planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded while the top grows in sun; Jackmanii is one of the oldest and most reliable large-flowered clematis cultivars, blooming on new growth so it can be pruned back hard each late winter.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool (mulch well or shade the base with low companion plants) while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis, fence, or other support. Introduced in England in 1862, Jackmanii is one of the most enduring and widely grown clematis cultivars ever bred, producing an abundance of large, velvety, deep purple flowers from early summer into fall. Because it flowers entirely on new growth, it belongs to the group of clematis that should be pruned hard, back to about a foot from the ground, in late winter, which keeps the vine vigorous and full of bloom rather than leggy and bare at the base. It is a tough, adaptable, long-lived vine that has introduced generations of gardeners to clematis.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Nelly Moser blooms on both old and new wood, so light pruning after the first flush rather than a hard cutback preserves the most flowers, and the pale flower color fades less in a site with some afternoon shade.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into a site with morning sun and afternoon shade, since Nelly Moser's flower color is prone to fading and bleaching in intense, all-day summer sun. Introduced in France in the 1890s, it remains one of the most recognizable clematis cultivars for its large, pale pink flowers boldly striped down the center of each petal with a deep carmine-rose bar. It flowers on old wood in late spring and can rebloom lightly on new growth later in summer, so pruning should be light, removing only dead or weak stems in late winter rather than cutting the whole vine back hard, which would sacrifice the main spring bloom.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Henryi blooms on old wood in late spring with a possible light rebloom on new growth, so prune only lightly to remove dead or weak stems rather than cutting the vine back hard.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis or fence. Henryi is one of the oldest and most classic large-flowered clematis cultivars, producing enormous, creamy white flowers with conspicuous chocolate-brown stamens that create a striking contrast against the pale petals. Because it flowers mainly on old wood from the previous season, heavy pruning removes the coming season's bloom, so gardeners should limit pruning to removing dead or damaged stems in late winter rather than cutting the whole plant back as with Jackmanii-type clematis. It has been a garden favorite for well over a century for its dependable, large-scale white flower display.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; unlike most clematis, Armand clematis is evergreen with leathery leaves and blooms very early in spring on the previous year's growth, so any pruning needed to control its size should happen right after flowering, not in late winter.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence able to support a large, vigorous evergreen vine. Native to China, Armand clematis is unusual among clematis for its leathery, glossy, evergreen leaves that provide year-round structure, and for its very early spring bloom of small, intensely fragrant white star-shaped flowers produced in such abundance that a mature vine can perfume an entire section of garden. It grows quickly and can become large and somewhat unruly if not given enough room or occasional pruning right after its spring bloom to keep it in bounds, since it flowers on the prior year's growth and heavy pruning at the wrong time removes the coming season's flowers. It is a good choice for screening a fence or arbor with year-round foliage in the milder parts of its range.

common_name: Madame Galen Trumpet Vine (Less-Aggressive Orange-Red Trumpet Creeper)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun on a strong, permanent support such as a large arbor or sturdy fence; Madame Galen is a hybrid trumpet vine that spreads less aggressively by root suckers than the straight native trumpet creeper, though it still grows vigorously.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun against a strong, permanent structure, since this vigorous woody vine becomes heavy over time and can damage weak supports or siding it is allowed to climb directly. A hybrid between American trumpet creeper and Chinese trumpet vine, Madame Galen produces abundant clusters of large, salmon-orange to apricot-red trumpet-shaped flowers through summer that are a favorite of hummingbirds. It is somewhat less prone to aggressive root suckering than the wild American species, though it still needs a firm hand with pruning to keep it in bounds and off of nearby structures. Once established it tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with ease, and a hard pruning in late winter keeps the vine full and encourages the current season's flowering growth.
